#### ABSTRACT

Implemented burns are a primary source of fire in natural systems and occur outside of the wildfire season. However, the impacts of fire season shift on native plant species are rarely studied. Understanding fire season effects are particularly important for managing threatened species, which are often the focus of managed burns. To assess the impacts of fire seasonality and identify potential limiting traits, I studied the threatened Leucopogon exolasius and two common congeners, all of which persist via fire-driven population dynamics. All species were monitored over a 16 year period to assess seedling survival, growth and primary juvenile period after fire. For L. exolasius and the common L. esquamatus, comparisons of survival, growth and maturation were made after winter and summer fires, to assess the effects of season of burn. A key difference was found in primary juvenile period, which was exceptionally long for L. exolasius (> 11 years for 80% of the population to flower) compared to the common congeners (3.2–7.57 years). Seasonal seed dormancy mechanisms meant that winter fires delayed emergence, leading to increases in primary juvenile period for both species. A long primary juvenile period may limit L. exolasius population persistence because plants are more likely to be killed by subsequent fire before maturation, while seasonal dormancy cues is a trait that would exacerbate the effects of this interval squeeze. In fire-prone systems, fire frequency is the key factor assumed to drive persistence, however, interactions with fire season can influence recruitment success. There are scant data on recruitment variation in response to fire seasonality, a factor that may have broad implications for rare and common species with seasonal germination requirements.

# 1. Introduction

Fire regime components include frequency, intensity (or severity) and season [\(Whelan, 1995; Hammill et al., 2016](#page-7-0)). The impact of fire frequency has been the focus of numerous studies, with a decrease in the intervals between fires limiting to obligate-seeding shrub species with long primary juvenile periods (e.g. [Santana et al., 2014](#page-6-0)). Projected changes to climate could exacerbate this interval squeeze [\(Enright](#page-6-1) [et al., 2015; Fairman et al., 2016\)](#page-6-1). Nevertheless, other fire regime factors, such as season and severity, can also undoubtedly affect plant population persistence and recovery (e.g. [Ooi et al., 2004, 2014; Liu](#page-6-2) [et al., 2005; Ooi, 2010; Céspedes et al., 2014; Hammill et al., 2016\)](#page-6-2) but there are few empirical studies measuring these effects over long time periods. Furthermore, managed burns are a primary source of fire in natural systems and are shifting fire season away from the peak time of natural wildfire. Understanding fire seasonality effects are particularly important for managing threatened species, however, the impacts of fire season shift on native plat populations are rarely studied.

In many fire-prone regions, fire causes plant mortality and

successful recruitment is restricted to the post-fire environment. For perennial species from such habitats, this means that long-term studies are required to understand population dynamics, because inter-fire periods can last for decades [\(Whelan, 1995](#page-7-0); [Menges and Quintana](#page-6-3) [Ascencio, 2004](#page-6-3)), and shifts between life-history stages may run over similar time scales. For example, gaining an estimate of primary juvenile period is important for determining the fire frequency that a species may be able to persist under ([Keith, 1996\)](#page-6-4). This can take from between two and 10 (or more) years for species in areas such as temperate Australia ([Benson, 1985; Burrows et al., 2008; Kubiak, 2009](#page-6-5)), where fire return intervals range from approximately seven to 30 years ([Bradstock and Gill, 2001; Lucas et al., 2007](#page-6-6)). Shorter term correlates of these measurements, such as size-class distributions for population age structure (e.g. [Ooi et al., 2007\)](#page-6-7), may be more easily achievable but do not provide the necessary resolution for parameterising predictive population models. However, long-term demographic studies, beyond a few years, are extremely rare.

Demographic studies are valuable for both the management of rare and threatened plant species, and predicting persistence [\(Schemske](#page-6-8)

{1}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

[et al., 1994; Menges et al., 2006; Keith et al., 2008](#page-6-8)). Comparative studies that investigate the biology of ecologically similar rare species and common congeners can help to detect possible limiting factors within the rare species [\(Kunin and Gaston, 1993; Bevill and Louda,](#page-6-9) [1999; Mattana et al., 2010](#page-6-9)). Although it is unlikely that generalisations exist regarding the causes of rarity [\(Gaston, 1994\)](#page-6-10), insights gained from data collected in comparative studies are particularly useful for the conservation of threatened species and the detection of broader ecological patterns [\(Bevill and, Louda, 1999; Lavergne et al., 2004\)](#page-6-11). These broader patterns may help to identify traits that could be limiting under changing environmental conditions, for both rare and common species, and provide insights to the evolutionary development of specific traits.

Regeneration from seeds is necessary for short-term regeneration and long-term persistence in fire-prone regions ([Whelan, 1995; Bond](#page-7-0) [and van Wilgen, 1996; Ooi et al., 2014](#page-7-0)). Plants that do not resprout, known as obligate-seeding species, are particularly dependent on recruitment from stored seed. As such, critical factors for the persistence of these species, and potential causes of rarity, are often related to seed ecology and recruitment stages [\(Burne et al., 2003; Risberg and](#page-6-12) [Granström, 2014\)](#page-6-12). Additionally, fire is the predominant driver of plant population dynamics in these regions and aspects of the fire regime itself needs to be considered as a potential contributor to rarity ([Burne](#page-6-12) [et al., 2003](#page-6-12)).

An increased use of managed fires, in addition to climate change, is causing a shift from current peak fire seasons, in addition to increasing the frequency of fire [\(McLoughlin, 1998; Williams et al., 2001; Cary](#page-6-13) [et al., 2006; Enright et al., 2015\)](#page-6-13). The threats caused by altered fire regimes may not only affect the persistence of those plant species that are already threatened with extinction, but also of many common species. Such common species may be at risk because they possess traits that have little plasticity in relation to projected changes. The most inflexible traits are likely to be those that are not adapted to current environmental conditions, but have ecologically fit well enough to have persisted. Evidence suggests that species composition within ecological communities may be strongly influenced by the relative abilities of species to cope with climate-driven changes ([Suttle et al., 2006\)](#page-6-14).

There is growing evidence that rates of extinction of plant species are increasing, across local and regional scales ([Thomas et al., 2004a;](#page-6-15) [Thuiller et al., 2005](#page-6-15)). This rate is influenced by human population growth, and the associated escalating demands on resources and climate-driven changes ([Gaston, 2005; Hahs et al., 2009](#page-6-16)). Species most at risk by the threat of extinction are those that are already rare, and therefore already limited in abundance and/or distribution [\(Gaston,](#page-6-10) [1994; Wilson et al., 2004](#page-6-10)). Understanding the possible anthropogenic and ecological causes of rarity are therefore crucial to designing and implementing conservation actions. In this study, I investigated postfire recruitment and development over a 16 year period for the species Leucopogon exolasius (F. Muell.) F. Muell. ex Benth. and the closely related common congeners L. setiger R. Br. and L. esquamatus R. Br. The demographic parameters following regeneration were compared between species in order to determine any potential causes of rarity for one of them, the threatened L. exolasius. All three species inhabit the fire-prone temperate sandstone vegetation around the Sydney region in south-eastern Australia, occurring on similar soil types and in similar micro-climates. The vegetation here is adapted to fire and there is a mean natural wildfire return interval ranging from approximately 14 to 20 years, a similar interval to shrublands in Mediterranean-climate regions in southwestern Australia [\(Miller and Murphy, 2018](#page-6-17)). Fires occur primarily in the hot late spring and summer periods (approximately November to February). The Sydney sandstone basin is one of several centres of high species richness and endemism on the Australian continent ([Crisp et al., 2001](#page-6-18)), but also highly urbanised. Prescribed fires are therefore implemented regularly to reduce fuel loads and protect assets, as well as for ecological purposes such as the conservation of biodiversity [\(Penman et al., 2011\)](#page-6-19).

Because limited abundance or distribution of plant species are

unlikely to be attributed to a single factor, investigations into several critical biological traits and life-history stages are the most likely to highlight limiting processes [\(Rabinowitz et al., 1984; Bevill and Louda,](#page-6-20) [1999\)](#page-6-20). Part of the benefit of using a small number of species in a comparative study, is that a larger number of factors may be examined with relative ease, and species can also be more easily selected to control for phylogenetic relatedness [\(Kunin and Gaston, 1993; Walck](#page-6-9) [et al., 2001\)](#page-6-9). Additionally, understanding demographic responses to environmental disturbance is crucial in habitats situated on the urban interface where the numbers of implemented fires are increasing ([McLoughlin, 1998\)](#page-6-13) and climate change is projected to drive changes to fire season and frequency [\(Williams et al., 2001; Cary et al., 2006;](#page-7-1) [Enright et al., 2015](#page-7-1)). I therefore assessed the demographic responses measured in the context of the fire regime to identify potential limiting traits. Specifically, I wanted to address the following questions:

- (1) How do key life-history stages of the three Leucopogon study species differ, and what are their responses to the fire regime, particularly season?
- (2) Can predicted changes to the fire regime potentially affect the persistence of the rare or common species studied?
- (3) Are there any identifiable factors that limit Leucopogon exolasius?

# 2. Materials and methods

# 2.1. Study species and sites

The Ericaceae family occurs in a number of habitats throughout the world floras including in South Africa and the Mediterranean Basin ([Ojeda et al., 1997\)](#page-6-21). In Australia, members compromise a significant part of the understorey in fire-prone plant communities. Leucopogon (Ericaceae) is a large genus consisting of about 230 species. This fireprone region of south-eastern Australia contains approximately 2000 plant species [\(Auld et al., 2000](#page-6-22)), and unlike its Mediterranean-type climate counterparts, has an aseasonal rainfall climate with no pronounced dry season, which may have consequences for the post-fire recovery of species with innate seasonal germination requirements ([Ooi, 2010](#page-6-23)). The three study species are all obligate-seeding woody shrubs with soil-stored seed banks ([Ooi et al., 2006a,b; 2007\)](#page-6-24). Although they do not co-occur at the same sites, they inhabit adjoining heath and woodland vegetation types, and have overlapping ranges. Leucopogon fruit are drupes and fresh exocarps of both L. exolasius and L. setiger are fleshy, while the endocarp is hard and lignified. Leucopogon esquamatus exocarp is papery and the endocarp comparatively more fibrous than hard [\(Ooi et al., 2006a\)](#page-6-24).

Leucopogon exolasius is an erect shrub that grows to approximately 2 m tall, and is a threatened species listed as 'vulnerable' both under the national Australian Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act (1999), and under the state of New South Wales (NSW) Threatened Species Conservation Act (1995). The species is endemic to the southern Sydney region of NSW and is restricted to approximately 14 known populations. It occurs in woodlands, and is restricted particularly to riverbank areas punctuated with outcropping sandstone. Leucopogon setiger, morphologically very similar to L. exolasius, is an erect shrub also approximately 2 m tall, and is distributed more widely ([Table 1](#page-2-0)), extending from the central western slopes of NSW to the coast. It is found in woodlands and open forest. Leucopogon esquamatus is a slender shrub, which grows to approximately 1 m tall. It is also widespread, occurring from the coast to the mountains (as for L. setiger), but extending south into the states of Victoria and Tasmania ([Table 1](#page-2-0)). It occurs in heath, woodlands and open forests. Taxonomy follows [Harden](#page-6-25) [\(1992\).](#page-6-25) Geographic distribution of each species were calculated using [IUCN \(2012\)](#page-6-26) criteria for extent of occurrence, which is defined as the area contained within the shortest continuous imaginary boundary which can be drawn to encompass all known sites of occurrence of a species.

{2}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

# 2.2. Background data

Reproductive attributes, including fecundity, seed viability, seed bank longevity, seed dormancy, germination, seedling survival and growth were collated from the literature and compared between all three species to identify limiting factors. Information on the habitat and substrate preferences of the study species, population structure, seed dormancy, seedling emergence phenology, seed bank longevity and seed viability were also included.

# 2.3. Study sites, habitat attributes and plant fecundity

Experimental data were collected from study sites located in the southern Sydney region, within Royal (34° 03′S, 151° 03′E) and Heathcote (34° 07′S, 150° 58′E) National Parks. The climate is temperate with no dry season (using the Köppen classification system). Average annual rainfall for the area is approximately 1050 mm distributed relatively evenly throughout the year, with the four highest monthly averages occurring in January, March, June and November. Average temperatures (maximum/minimum) are approximately 27/ 18 °C and 16/6 °C in summer and winter respectively.

A 30 m × 30 m plot was marked out at two study sites for each species. At each plot, the type of vegetation, slope and aspect were recorded. All individuals within the plots, covering a range of size classes, were tagged using stainless steel wire stakes with numbered brass tags. For each tagged plant, height (or stem length if not vertical), canopy area (calculated as an ellipse from two measurements at right angles) and the presence or absence of buds or flowers were recorded to estimate fecundity of mature populations during late spring. To enable comparisons between sites and species, the numbers of fruit per 0.1 m2 of canopy were calculated for each plant. Data were tested for homogeneity of variance using Levene's test. Comparisons were conducted using a two-factor nested analysis of variance (ANOVA), with species treated as a fixed factor and site as a random factor, using SYSTAT.

For each species, seedling survival and growth experiments were designed so that plots at each of the two sites were burnt during a summer wildfire in 2001/02. Up to 25 permanent 1 m × 1 m quadrats were located under or near canopies of mature individuals within each plot, as seedling emergence had previously been observed occurring primarily within a few metres of adult canopies. Nearby (or adjacent) plots to the above summer wildfires had been burnt by a prescribed winter fire in 1999, at a single site for both L. exolasius and L. esquamatus. The summer wildfire was of very high intensity, occurring during extreme fire weather conditions, while the prescribed winter hazard reduction burn was of much lower intensity. However the quadrats observed after both fires had all been completely scorched. Total number of quadrats followed at each site, and the season of burn, are shown in [Table 1](#page-2-0).

# 2.4. Post-fire seedling survival and early growth

After fire, quadrats were inspected regularly for signs of seedling emergence [\(Ooi et al., 2004](#page-6-2)). Once emerged, all seedlings within quadrats were tagged. Time of emergence and seedling height were recorded upon tagging. Survival and height were subsequently recorded at the end of each summer and each winter for four years, as this was considered the time most likely for mortality to occur. Seedling survival and seedling heights were analysed at the end of the fourth summer using SYSTAT. Due to a small number of seedlings surviving in some plots, I first used using a one-factor ANOVA comparing seedling survival among species after four years (no differences found between species F2,3 < 0.06, P > 0.940). However, scrutiny if the data suggested there was large variation between sites for each species, so to test for possible site effects, a two-factor ANOVA without replication, with year and site as factors, was used. This approach does not allow testing of significance of the interaction and a cautious approach is recommended for testing the significance of main effects ([Zar, 1984](#page-7-2)). The significance levels were therefore increased to 0.01.

# 2.5. Primary juvenile period

Seedlings were tagged and survival and growth followed from 2002 to 2016 after the 2001/02 summer fire to determine primary juvenile period. This was assessed each year for the first four years, and then in 2006, 2009, 2012, 2014 and 2016. The time taken for tagged individuals to flower was recorded. Data from occasional years were missed, however multiple years over time were still recorded until maturity for all species. The total number of individuals assessed changed over time due to mortality, with the original number of seedlings tagged ranging from 33 (L. exolasius) to 151 (L. esquamatus). By the time approximately 80% of the population was in flower, total number of individuals surviving varied among species (L. exolasius, 7–12; L. setiger,8–13; L. esquamatus 12–55). Data were analysed using a binomial Generalised Linear Mixed Model (GLMM), with site included as a random factor, to determine if the time taken to mature differed between species. The logistic models fitted for each species were used to estimate the time taken for 50% and 80% of the population to reach maturity (i.e. flowered). Analyses were conducted using the lmer4 package in R [\(R Core Team, 2015](#page-6-27)).

### 2.6. Comparison of growth and primary juvenile period: winter vs summer fire

The effect of different fire seasons on seedling survival and growth was also investigated. The prescribed winter fire in 1999 that had burnt a single site for both L. exolasius and L. esquamatus meant that withinsite comparisons could be made for these species after this fire and the 2001/2 summer wildfire event. Growth was followed for 16 years after the winter fire (seedlings emerged in 2000) and 14 years after the

A previous study ([Ooi, 2010\)](#page-6-23) reported some results from the winter fire for L. esquamatus, and was used in the interpretation of the current study. The effect of fire season on reproductive output was also estimated for L. exolasius by comparing canopy area for plants emerging after post-winter and post-summer burns.

### 3. Results

# 3.1. Comparison of background data

The collation of background data revealed a number of similarities between species. All species occur within the temperate climate zone, with no seasonal rainfall pattern. The two common species extend into regions with warmer (north) and cooler (south and/or higher altitude) overall temperatures. All species occur on similar low nutrient soils. They also occur in similar woodland habitats, although L. esquamatus is more dominant in heath than woodland and L. exolasius is restricted mainly to rocky areas near creeks and rivers ([Table 1\)](#page-2-0).

Although diaspore weights differ amongst species, seed weights (embryo and endosperm) were very similar, as are seed embryo morphologies [\(Table 2](#page-3-0)). All species displayed high levels of fecundity. Leucopogon esquamatus produced significantly more fruit per canopy area than the other two species (F2,4 = 32.624, P = 0.004), however, mean canopy area of mature L. esquamatus individuals was also smallest by at least an order of magnitude [\(Table 2\)](#page-3-0). As a result, the overall production of seeds per plant varies little between the three study species. For each species, there were no significant differences found between study sites (F3,47 = 0.398, P < 0.755). Flowering phenology and likely pollinators are similar due to very similar flower morphology, as are the seed maturation times. Seed viability is also high for all species [\(Table 3](#page-4-0)), and consistently highest for the rare L. exolasius.

All three species have been classified as morphophysiologically dormant and require stratification at seasonal temperatures to overcome dormancy [\(Ooi et al., 2006a\)](#page-6-24). Emergence in the field is therefore seasonal, with seedlings appearing at the same time of year (peaking in autumn/early winter), even if there is significant rainfall at other times of the year. Recruitment has been recorded to mainly occur after fire

with seedling emergence still restricted to same emergence season ([Table 3\)](#page-4-0). Some inter-fire recruitment had also been recorded [\(Ooi](#page-6-28) [et al., 2006b\)](#page-6-28).

Emus (Dromaius novaehollandiae) were identified from the literature as a species that had a preference for drupaceous fruit of Leucopogon and other Ericaceae [\(Keighery, 1996;](#page-6-29) [Quin, 1996; McGrath and Bass, 1999; Calviño-Cancela et al. 2006](#page-6-29)). Numbers of ericaceous fruit found in emu scats, studied in both eastern and south-western Australia, were orders of magnitude greater than that of any other species. # 3.2. With regards to seedling heights, Leucopogon esquamatus was significantly smaller than the other two species after 4 years growth (F2,164 = 7.062, P = 0.001) [\(Table 3](#page-4-0)). # 3.3. Primary juvenile period There was a significant effect of species on primary juvenile period (χ2 = 504.24, P < 0.001). All species differed significantly from each other (P < 0.001) [\(Fig. 1](#page-4-1)). 1	Aust. J. Bot., 1983, 31, 293-6
2	
3	# Relationship between Time Since the Last Fire and Flowering in *Telopea speciosissima* R. Br. and *Lambertia formosa* Sm.
4	
5	*Graham H. Pyke*
6	
7	The Australian Museum, 6-8 College St, Sydney, N.S.W., 2000.
8	
9	## Abstract
10	
11	For *Telopea speciosissima* the percentage (or density) of plants in flower, the average number of flowers per inflorescence and the average number of fruits per inflorescence all appear to peak 2 years after a summer fire and decline thereafter. On the other hand, the average height of the inflorescences above the ground increases with time since the last fire. For *Lambertia formosa* the density of inflorescences appears to reach a peak 2 or 3 years after a summer fire.
12	
13	## Introduction
14	
15	The effects of fire on the Australian flora are many and are increasingly well studied (see Gill *et al.* 1981). There appears, however, to be little quantitative information on the relationships between time since the last fire and flowering of Australian plants (Gill 1981; Specht 1981). Only for *Xanthorrhoea australis* is there a well established relationship (Specht *et al.* 1958; Garnet 1971; Gill and Ingwersen 1976; Gill 1981): in some places this species flowers only rarely in the absence of fire (Specht *et al.* 1958; Garnet 1971).
16	
17	The aim of this paper is to analyse spatial and temporal variation in flowering of *Telopea speciosissima* (waratah) and *Lambertia formosa* with respect to time since the last fire. This analysis is possible as a result of studies on the pollination biology of these plants and the foraging ecology of honeyeaters that visit them for nectar (Pyke 1980, 1981*a*, 1981*b*).
18	
19	## Methods
20	
21	The data presented were collected between December 1979 and December 1981 in the Brisbane Water National Park (lat. 33°32′22″S., long. 151°16′56″E.; elevation 170 m above sea level) and Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park (lat. 33°36′18″S., long. 151°16′16″E.; elevation 145 m above sea level). In each region, study sites are located in plateau-type, low open-forest (Benson and Fallding 1981) dominated by *Eucalyptus gummifera* (Gaertn.) Hochr., *E. haemastoma* Sm. and *E. oblonga* DC., with a shrub understory composed mainly of *Lambertia formosa* Sm. Both regions are located on plateau tops and hence all study sites have the same aspect. In both regions soils are deep, yellow and earthy (Benson and Fallding 1981) with no apparent differences between the study sites.
22	
23	The Brisbane Water study site contains two areas in terms of fire history: one area last burnt in December 1976, the other in December 1979. The two areas are separated by a vehicle trail which stopped the more recent fire from spreading further. There are no apparent differences between the two areas in terms of soil or vegetation. The entire Ku-ring-gai Chase study site last burnt in 1965.
24	
25	Flowering in *Telopea speciosissima* has been recorded in two ways. In the 1976 burn study area in Brisbane Water National Park, the total number of flowering plants was recorded for the spring flowering periods of 1979, 1980 and 1981. For each inflorescence
26	
27	0067-1924/83/030293$02.00
28	
29	<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
30	
31	294 G. H. Pyke
32	
33	the total number of flowers, height above the ground and number of fruits were also recorded. In each year peak flowering occurred about mid September with high synchrony among plants. In this area and in the other two study areas, permanent circular plots of 20 m radius were established and the numbers of flowering plants within these circles counted every 3 weeks during spring 1981. The numbers of non-flowering plants in each circle were also recorded for spring 1981. Flowering in *Lambertia formosa* was recorded by counting the number of inflorescences in each circle during spring 1981 and in two of the present Brisbane Water circles during spring 1980. During spring 1981, there were four circles in the Brisbane Water area of the 1976 fire, two in the area of the 1979 fire and two in the Ku-ring-gai Chase area.
34	
35	## Results
36	
37	### *Flowering of* Telopea *in Successive Years*
38	
39	In the Brisbane Water area which last burnt in December 1976, the total number of flowering *Telopea* plants has declined dramatically since spring 1979 (Table 1). Since spring
40	
41	**Table 1. Flowering of *Telopea speciosissima* in areas of 1976 and 1979 fires during successive years**
42	
43	| Area | Flowering time | Total No. of flowering plants | Mean No. of flowers per inflorescence | Mean inflorescence ht (cm) | Mean No. of fruit per inflorescence |
44	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
45	| 1976 fire | Spring 1979 | 306 | 79·5±0·9 | 162·4±2·5 | 2·45±0·11 |
46	| 1976 fire | Spring 1980 | 100 | 64·9±1·4 | 186·0±3·4 | 0·86±0·11 |
47	| 1976 fire | Spring 1981 | 9 | 62·3±3·0 | 228·8±13·3 | 0·56±0·24 |
48	| 1979 fire | Spring 1981 | Sample size 63 | 171·8±4·2 | 138·7±3·1 | 3·74±0·41 |
49	
50	1979 there have also been decreases in the average number of flowers per inflorescence and in the average number of fruit per inflorescence and increases in the average inflorescence height. The differences between 1979 and 1980 are all significant (*P*<0·05, *t*-test); for 1980 and 1981 only the difference in mean inflorescence height is significant (*P*<0·05, *t*-test). During spring 1981 in the circles in the 1979 fire area (see Table 1), the inflorescence height averaged less than for any of the flowering periods in the 1976 fire area (*P*<0·05, *t*-test) while the numbers of flowers and fruits per inflorescence averaged more (*P*<0·05, *t*-test).
51	
52	### *Flowering of* Telopea *in Different Places*
53	
54	During spring 1981 the density of flowering plants (i.e. number of flowering plants per circle) and the percentage of plants in flower declined with increases in the time since an area last burnt (Table 2). The differences in the percentage of flowering are significant between the 1979 and 1976 (or 1965) burn areas (*P*<0·05, *t*-test based on Normal approximation to binomial) but not between the 1965 and 1976 burn areas (*P*>0·05, *t*-test based on Normal approximation to binomial).
55	
56	### *Flowering of* Lambertia
57	
58	During spring 1981 the peak density of *Lambertia* inflorescences declined with increases in the time since an area last burnt (Table 3). The differences between the areas are significantly different (*P*<0·05 for comparisons between 1979 and 1976 burn areas and between 1976 and 1965 burn areas, *t*-test).
59	
60	For two circles in the 1976 burn area, the peak numbers of *Lambertia* inflorescences declined significantly from spring 1980 to spring 1981 (*P*<0·05, *t*-test) (Table 3).
61	
62	<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
63	
64	Fire and Flowering in *Telopea* and *Lambertia* 295
65	
66	## Discussion
67	
68	There appear to be strong relationships between flowering and time since the last fire for both *Telopea* and *Lambertia*. In the case of *Telopea*, the percentage (or density) of plants in flower, the average number of flowers per inflorescence and the average number of fruits per inflorescence all peak 2 years after a summer fire and decline thereafter (Tables
69	
70	**Table 2. Flowering of *Telopea speciosissima* in different areas during spring 1981**
71	
72	| Area | No. of circles | Mean No. of flowering plants per circle | Mean No. of plants per circle | Percentage of plants in flower |
73	|---|---|---|---|---|
74	| Ku-ring-gai Chase (1965 fire) | 2 | 0·50 | 32·5±5·5 | 1·5 (*n*=65) |
75	| Brisbane Water (1976 fire) | 4 | 0·75 | 138·8±19·4 | 0·5 (*n*=555) |
76	| Brisbane Water (1979 fire) | 2 | 23·00 | 105·0±2·0 | 22·0 (*n*=210) |

Aust. J. Bot., 1983, 31, 293-6

# Relationship between Time Since the Last Fire and Flowering in *Telopea speciosissima* R. Br. and *Lambertia formosa* Sm.

*Graham H. Pyke*

The Australian Museum, 6-8 College St, Sydney, N.S.W., 2000.

## Abstract

For *Telopea speciosissima* the percentage (or density) of plants in flower, the average number of flowers per inflorescence and the average number of fruits per inflorescence all appear to peak 2 years after a summer fire and decline thereafter. On the other hand, the average height of the inflorescences above the ground increases with time since the last fire. For *Lambertia formosa* the density of inflorescences appears to reach a peak 2 or 3 years after a summer fire.

## Introduction

The effects of fire on the Australian flora are many and are increasingly well studied (see Gill *et al.* 1981). There appears, however, to be little quantitative information on the relationships between time since the last fire and flowering of Australian plants (Gill 1981; Specht 1981). Only for *Xanthorrhoea australis* is there a well established relationship (Specht *et al.* 1958; Garnet 1971; Gill and Ingwersen 1976; Gill 1981): in some places this species flowers only rarely in the absence of fire (Specht *et al.* 1958; Garnet 1971).

The aim of this paper is to analyse spatial and temporal variation in flowering of *Telopea speciosissima* (waratah) and *Lambertia formosa* with respect to time since the last fire. This analysis is possible as a result of studies on the pollination biology of these plants and the foraging ecology of honeyeaters that visit them for nectar (Pyke 1980, 1981*a*, 1981*b*).

## Methods

The data presented were collected between December 1979 and December 1981 in the Brisbane Water National Park (lat. 33°32′22″S., long. 151°16′56″E.; elevation 170 m above sea level) and Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park (lat. 33°36′18″S., long. 151°16′16″E.; elevation 145 m above sea level). In each region, study sites are located in plateau-type, low open-forest (Benson and Fallding 1981) dominated by *Eucalyptus gummifera* (Gaertn.) Hochr., *E. haemastoma* Sm. and *E. oblonga* DC., with a shrub understory composed mainly of *Lambertia formosa* Sm. Both regions are located on plateau tops and hence all study sites have the same aspect. In both regions soils are deep, yellow and earthy (Benson and Fallding 1981) with no apparent differences between the study sites.

The Brisbane Water study site contains two areas in terms of fire history: one area last burnt in December 1976, the other in December 1979. The two areas are separated by a vehicle trail which stopped the more recent fire from spreading further. There are no apparent differences between the two areas in terms of soil or vegetation. The entire Ku-ring-gai Chase study site last burnt in 1965.

Flowering in *Telopea speciosissima* has been recorded in two ways. In the 1976 burn study area in Brisbane Water National Park, the total number of flowering plants was recorded for the spring flowering periods of 1979, 1980 and 1981. For each inflorescence

0067-1924/83/030293$02.00

<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

294 G. H. Pyke

the total number of flowers, height above the ground and number of fruits were also recorded. In each year peak flowering occurred about mid September with high synchrony among plants. In this area and in the other two study areas, permanent circular plots of 20 m radius were established and the numbers of flowering plants within these circles counted every 3 weeks during spring 1981. The numbers of non-flowering plants in each circle were also recorded for spring 1981. Flowering in *Lambertia formosa* was recorded by counting the number of inflorescences in each circle during spring 1981 and in two of the present Brisbane Water circles during spring 1980. During spring 1981, there were four circles in the Brisbane Water area of the 1976 fire, two in the area of the 1979 fire and two in the Ku-ring-gai Chase area.

## Results

### *Flowering of* Telopea *in Successive Years*

In the Brisbane Water area which last burnt in December 1976, the total number of flowering *Telopea* plants has declined dramatically since spring 1979 (Table 1). Since spring

**Table 1. Flowering of *Telopea speciosissima* in areas of 1976 and 1979 fires during successive years**

| Area | Flowering time | Total No. of flowering plants | Mean No. of flowers per inflorescence | Mean inflorescence ht (cm) | Mean No. of fruit per inflorescence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1976 fire | Spring 1979 | 306 | 79·5±0·9 | 162·4±2·5 | 2·45±0·11 |
| 1976 fire | Spring 1980 | 100 | 64·9±1·4 | 186·0±3·4 | 0·86±0·11 |
| 1976 fire | Spring 1981 | 9 | 62·3±3·0 | 228·8±13·3 | 0·56±0·24 |
| 1979 fire | Spring 1981 | Sample size 63 | 171·8±4·2 | 138·7±3·1 | 3·74±0·41 |

1979 there have also been decreases in the average number of flowers per inflorescence and in the average number of fruit per inflorescence and increases in the average inflorescence height. The differences between 1979 and 1980 are all significant (*P*<0·05, *t*-test); for 1980 and 1981 only the difference in mean inflorescence height is significant (*P*<0·05, *t*-test). During spring 1981 in the circles in the 1979 fire area (see Table 1), the inflorescence height averaged less than for any of the flowering periods in the 1976 fire area (*P*<0·05, *t*-test) while the numbers of flowers and fruits per inflorescence averaged more (*P*<0·05, *t*-test).

### *Flowering of* Telopea *in Different Places*

During spring 1981 the density of flowering plants (i.e. number of flowering plants per circle) and the percentage of plants in flower declined with increases in the time since an area last burnt (Table 2). The differences in the percentage of flowering are significant between the 1979 and 1976 (or 1965) burn areas (*P*<0·05, *t*-test based on Normal approximation to binomial) but not between the 1965 and 1976 burn areas (*P*>0·05, *t*-test based on Normal approximation to binomial).

### *Flowering of* Lambertia

During spring 1981 the peak density of *Lambertia* inflorescences declined with increases in the time since an area last burnt (Table 3). The differences between the areas are significantly different (*P*<0·05 for comparisons between 1979 and 1976 burn areas and between 1976 and 1965 burn areas, *t*-test).

For two circles in the 1976 burn area, the peak numbers of *Lambertia* inflorescences declined significantly from spring 1980 to spring 1981 (*P*<0·05, *t*-test) (Table 3).

<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

Fire and Flowering in *Telopea* and *Lambertia* 295

## Discussion

There appear to be strong relationships between flowering and time since the last fire for both *Telopea* and *Lambertia*. In the case of *Telopea*, the percentage (or density) of plants in flower, the average number of flowers per inflorescence and the average number of fruits per inflorescence all peak 2 years after a summer fire and decline thereafter (Tables

**Table 2. Flowering of *Telopea speciosissima* in different areas during spring 1981**

| Area | No. of circles | Mean No. of flowering plants per circle | Mean No. of plants per circle | Percentage of plants in flower |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ku-ring-gai Chase (1965 fire) | 2 | 0·50 | 32·5±5·5 | 1·5 (*n*=65) |
| Brisbane Water (1976 fire) | 4 | 0·75 | 138·8±19·4 | 0·5 (*n*=555) |
| Brisbane Water (1979 fire) | 2 | 23·00 | 105·0±2·0 | 22·0 (*n*=210) |

**Table 3. Flowering of *Lambertia formosa* in different areas during spring 1980 and 1981**

| Area | Peak No. of inflorescences per circle 1980: Mean | 1980: s.e. | 1980: *n* | 1981: Mean | 1981: s.e. | 1981: *n* |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ku-ring-gai Chase (1965 fire) | — | — | — | 5·5 | 3·5 | 2 |
| Brisbane Water (1976 fire) | 195·5 | 17·5 | 2 | 96·5 | 7·8 | 4 |
| Brisbane Water (1979 fire) | — | — | — | 419·0 | 108·0 | 2 |

1 and 2). On the other hand, the average height of the inflorescences above the ground appears to increase with increases in time since the last fire (Table 1). This undoubtedly reflects the continual growth of the plants, starting from a rhizome, following a fire. The density of *Lambertia* inflorescences reaches a peak 2 or 3 years after a summer fire (Table 3). No information is currently available on either the cause or the adaptive significance of these relationships.

## Acknowledgments

This research was supported by a grant from the Australian Research Grants Committee. Permission to carry out research within National Parks was kindly provided by the N.S.W. National Parks and Wildlife Service. Two anonymous referees provided many helpful comments on an earlier version of this paper.

Garnet, J. R. (1971). 'The Wildflowers of Wilsons Promontory National Park.' (Lothian Publ. Co. and Field Nat. Club: Melbourne.)

Gill, A. M. (1981). Adaptive responses of Australian vascular plant species to fires. In 'Fire and the Australian Biota', eds A. M. Gill, R. H. Groves and I. R. Noble. (Aust. Acad. Sci.: Canberra.)

<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

296 G. H. Pyke

Gill, A. M., Groves, R. H., and Noble, I. R. (eds) (1981). 'Fire and the Australian Biota.' (Aust. Acad. Sci.: Canberra.)

Gill, A. M., and Ingwersen, F. (1976). Growth of *Xanthorrhoea australis* R. Br. in relation to fire. *J. Appl. Ecol.* 13, 195-203.

Pyke, G. H. (1981*b*). Honeyeater foraging: a test of optimal foraging theory. *Anim. Behav.* 29, 878-88.

Specht, R. L. (1981). Responses to fires in heathlands and related shrublands. In 'Fire and the Australian Biota', eds A. M. Gill, R. H. Groves and I. R. Noble. (Aust. Acad. Sci.: Canberra.)

5	# **INTRODUCTION**
6	
7	The natural fire regimes of the treeless high mountain vegetation of Australia are difficult to quantify, and the role of fire in the dynamics of alpine and subalpine vegetation in Australia is largely unknown. At the landscape scale (that of square kilometres or more), fire appears to be relatively rare in these environments (Kirkpatrick & Dickinson 1984; Leigh *et al*. 1987; Wimbush & Forrester 1988; Williams & Costin 1994). Given that few fires have occurred in alpine and subalpine vegetation, knowledge of post-fire ecology, especially initial impacts and early responses, in alpine and treeless subalpine vegetation is also scant.

Prior to European settlement, landscape-scale fires are likely to have occurred in high mountain treeless vegetation in mainland Australia only once or twice per century (Leigh *et al*. 1987). 11	# Early post-fire regeneration in subalpine heathland and grassland in the Victorian Alpine National Park, south-eastern Australia
12	
13	C-H. A. WAHREN,1† W. A. PAPST2‡ AND R. J. WILLIAMS<sup>3</sup> \*
14	
15	1 *Department of Agricultural Sciences, La Trobe University, Victoria,* <sup>2</sup> *Centre for Land Protection Research, Bendigo, Victoria and* <sup>3</sup> *CSIRO Sustainable Ecosystems, PMB 44, Winnellie Northern Territory 0822, Australia (Email: dick.williams@terc.csiro.au)*
16	
17	**Abstract** Landscape fire (at the scale of square kilometres or more) is relatively rare in the alpine and subalpine environments of Australia. In early 1998, a major fire (the 'Caledonia Fire'), burnt approximately 35 000 ha, of which approximately 3000 hectares was subalpine heathland, grassland and wetland within the Victorian Alpine National Park. This fire was one of only three landscape-scale fires that have occurred anywhere in the treeless vegetation of the Victorian Alps in the past 100 years, the others being in 1939 and 1985. Monitoring of regeneration in subalpine vegetation commenced 3 weeks postfire. Sites were established in burnt grassland at Holmes Plain (1400 m a.s.l.) and burnt grassland and heathland at Wellington Plain (1480 m a.s.l.), and in unburnt grassland at both sites. In burnt grassland and heathland, the fire consumed much of the vegetation, leaving extensive areas of bare ground. The cover of dense vegetation declined from > 70% prefire, to approximately 15% immediately postfire. Bare ground at the Holmes and Wellington Plains sites ranged from 70% to 85% immediately postfire. By May 2000, approximately 2.5 years postfire, dense vegetation cover in grassland had increased to approximately 20%, and bare ground had decreased to an average of approximately 30%. In unburnt grassland, dense vegetation cover was generally > 95%, and the amount of bare ground less than 5%. The tussock-forming snow grasses resprouted vigorously following fire, and had flowered prolifically after 1 year. In heathland, most of the shrubs were incinerated, leaving close to 100% bare soil. Since then, a number of grasses and some dominant shrubs have resprouted vigorously, with some seedling regeneration. By May 2000, in heathland, bare soil was still > 50% and dense vegetation < 20%. Such ground cover conditions during this early postfire period were well below prefire levels, and well below the levels necessary to protect alpine soils from erosion. The Caledonia Fire has provided a rare opportunity to study ecological processes associated with postfire regeneration in treeless subalpine landscapes.
18	
19	**Key words**: alpine, bare ground, biomass, Caledonia Fire, catchment protection, disturbance, fire regime, litter, vegetation cover.

30	
31	1954; Carr & Turner 1959a; Lawrence 1999). These practices all increased the frequency of fire in alpine and subalpine vegetation (Pryor 1939; Stretton 1946; Raeder-Roitzsch & Phillips 1958; Leigh *et al*. 1987; Banks 1989; Kershaw & Strickland 1989; Lawrence 1999). On mainland Australia, prescribed fire in treeless subalpine and alpine vegetation was banned in the 1940s and 1950s, as its use was linked clearly to land degradation in the high mountain catchments (Australian Academy of Science 1957; Costin *et al*. 1959; Williams & Costin 1994).
32	
33	In Victoria, there are few detailed data on the occurrence of fires and their effects on alpine and subalpine plant communities. Extensive fires in treeless vegetation are known to have occurred on two occasions in the 20th century. According to Carr & Turner (1959a) '. . . small fires spread onto the high plains from the neighbouring slopes prior to 1939, such as in 1926, but these fires were of minor importance'. In contrast, the State-wide fires of 1939 burnt approximately 80% of the snow gum country on the Bogong High Plains above approximately 1500 m a.s.l. (Carr & Turner 1959a). Although these fires burnt much treeless subalpine and alpine vegetation, that is, heathland, grassland, and wetland (Carr & Turner 1959a), we do not know the precise extent or severity of these fires. In 1985, a fire at Mount Buffalo burnt approximately 11 000 ha of lowland and forested foothill vegetation, and approximately 150 ha of treeless subalpine heathland, grassland and wetland (Wahren *et al*. 1999). The subject of the present paper is an extensive fire that occurred in the south-eastern parts of the Victorian Alpine National Park in January 1998: the 'Caledonia Fire'.
34	
35	Subsequent to the last glaciation, Australian alpine environments have evolved in response to relatively small-scale disturbances (1 m<sup>2</sup> –1 ha) such as localized frost heave, wind blasting and insect herbivory. Larger scale disturbances such as fire and extensive grazing by large vertebrate herbivores over square kilometres of country are rare or non-existent (Williams 1990; Williams & Costin 1994). Under such a native regime of small-scale disturbances, Australian alpine environments are characterized by a high cover of vegetation (normally close to 100%) and relatively little exposed bare soil (< 1–2%; Australian Academy of Science 1957; Costin 1958; Williams & Costin 1994). The removal of vegetation and litter by fire, and the consequent exposure of bare soil, has major implications in Australian alpine landscapes, because exposure of alpine soils is undesirable for soil conservation purposes, and subsequent regeneration to adequate soil cover is slow (Wahren *et al*. 1994; Williams & Costin 1994).
36	
37	In the present paper, we summarize the early postfire changes in vegetation and ground cover conditions that have occurred in grassland and heathland on Holmes and Wellington Plains, two of the larger high plains burnt in the Caledonia Fire (Fig. 1). We focus on the first 2 years post-fire because there have been no detailed, quantitative studies of early post-fire responses in Australian alpine landscapes following fires of such magnitude. The specific aim is to document the changes in vegetation cover, the amount of bare ground, and changes to gaps that have occurred in grassland and heathland over the first 2 years post-fire. Both communities are extensive in treeless high mountain environments in Australia. Within each, the amount of bare ground and both the quality and quantity of vegetation cover, and the nature of gaps created by the death of grass tussocks or shrubs, are critical determinants of both vegetation change and landscape condition in Australian high mountain landscapes (Wahren *et al*. 1994; Williams & Costin 1994).
38	
39	#### **Fire and study sites**
40	
41	The Caledonia Fire started on 31 December 1997, from an abandoned campfire on the Caledonia River, in mixed lowland eucalypt forest. 1 January 1998 was a day of extreme fire weather: the predicted forest fire danger index (Luke & McArthur 1978) for the nearby town of Heyfield was 50 (Tolhurst 1998). Fire weather and drought conditions at this time were broadly similar to those of other years in the past century when widespread fires occurred in Victoria: 1983, 1967, 1964, 1939 and 1926 (McCarthy & Tolhurst 2000). The fire burnt approximately 35 000 ha of the Carey Forest, of which approximately 22 000 ha was within the Alpine National Park, and approximately 3000 ha was treeless subalpine vegetation.
42	
43	The landscape above approximately 1400 m is a mosaic of high ridges, wooded slopes, rolling grassy plains and wetlands. The treeless plains and surrounding snow gum (*Eucalyptus pauciflora*) woodlands have been grazed during summer and autumn by free ranging cattle since the late 19th century and cattle were present at the time of the fire. Sporadic grazing continued for 3 months post-fire, but grazing was excluded from the fire-affected area for the 1998–1999 and 1999–2000 seasons.
44	
45	The fires were intense crown fires in both the eucalypt forests of the foothills and the subalpine snow gum woodlands. In the treeless vegetation, fire intensity was unknown, but field observations indicated that the fire at Wellington Plain was more intense and burnt more of the vegetation than at Holmes Plain. At Holmes and Wellington Plains, > 90% of the grassland, heathland and snow gum woodlands were burnt, and the subalpine bogs were also extensively burnt. This represents the most extensive fire in alpine and subalpine vegetation since 1939 (McCarthy & Tolhurst 2000).
46	
47	{2}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
48	
49	# **METHODS**
50	
51	#### **Monitoring sites**
52	
53	At the end of January 1998, 3 weeks after the fire, monitoring sites were established at Holmes Plain (146°45-14--E, 37°24-32--S; 1400 m a.s.l.) and Wellington Plain (146°49-54--E, 37°29-46--S; 1480 m a.s.l.). These plains were selected because they were representative of the extensive subalpine high plains in this region of the Victorian Alps (Walsh *et al*. 1984, 1986) and, in the case of Holmes Plain, because two sites had been established in grassland in 1991 as part of a general monitoring program in the high country. At both sites, the soil was alpine humus soil, a wellstructured organic loam that is acid, nutrient poor, and is typical of most alpine and subalpine grasslands and heathlands in mainland Australia (Williams & Costin 1994). One of these sites was burnt, the other was outside the fire perimeter; both sites were used for the present study. Extra sites were established in burnt heathland and grassland at both Holmes and Wellington Plains, and in an unburnt area of grassland at Wellington Plain, close to the burnt grassland. This unburnt grassland was within the fire perimeter. Using this network of sites, the changes in the burnt grassland over time could be compared with those in longunburnt grassland. Unfortunately, there were no suitable unburnt heathland sites.
54	
55	# **Estimation of ground cover and biomass**
56	
57	Point quadrats, sampled along permanent transects (Kent & Coker 1992), were used to record species composition and ground cover conditions. Transects were 10 m long with points 4 mm in diameter, and 20 cm apart (50 points per transect). This method has been widely used for many decades to estimate the cover of individual species and life forms (grasses, forbs and shrubs) in treeless vegetation in Australia (Carr & Turner 1959b; Wimbush & Costin 1979a,b,c; Wahren *et al*. 1994). Ground cover at each point was rated in terms of three cover classes (Wahren *et al*. 1994). Cover class 1 (CC1) is fixed litter or dense live vegetation, cover class (CC2) provides intermediate vegetation cover but the litter is loose, and cover class (CC3) consists of bare ground or sparse vegetation and/or thin (< 5 mm thick) loose litter. Live vegetation and litter were measured together in all cover classes, as both are important for soil protection in Australian alpine environments (Wahren *et al*. 1994).
58	
59	In the Holmes Plain grassland, there were 40 transects (including 13 from 1991) distributed over an area of approximately 40 ha of burnt grassland. There were an additional 10 transects (six from 1991) in the unburnt grassland, over an area of approximately 2 ha; burnt and unburnt grassland sites were approximately 1 km apart. At Wellington Plain, there were 40 transects established in burnt heathland over an area of approximately 40 ha, and 10 transects in burnt grassland over an area of 2 ha. Subsequent to January 1998, the vegetation was remeasured along the transects in May 1998, January, May and December 1999, and late April/early May 2000. In December 1999, four transects were set up in a patch of unburnt grassland at Wellington Plain, 200 m from the burnt grassland; these were remeasured in May 2000.
60	
61	Above-ground biomass was sampled in March–May 2000, using direct harvest from 10 0.25-m<sup>2</sup> quadrats distributed at random in both burnt and unburnt grassland of Holmes and Wellington Plains. Samples were separated in the field into standing vegetation and litter components. Biomass samples were not collected from heathland because of the likely damage to regenerating areas where there was at least 50% bare ground and small shrub seedlings.
62	
63	#### **Assessment of grass tussock basal area, intertussock gaps and prefire shrub cover**
64	
65	In addition to changes in bare ground and vegetation cover, we documented changes in the size and type of gap, both interdominant and within-canopy, in grassland and heathland. Such gaps are important determinants of ecological processes in these communities (Williams & Ashton 1988; Williams 1992). The area occupied by intertussock gaps and *Poa* tussock bases was estimated by line intercepts (Bonham 1989). Intercepted basal tussock length was measured by using a metal pin, 4 mm in diameter, placed vertically against the edge of the tussock. Ten randomly distributed 10-m long transects were sampled in both burnt and unburnt grassland at Holmes Plain, and in burnt grassland at Wellington Plain. As there were no prefire data of shrub cover in open heathland, this was estimated at Holmes Plain by using line intercepts to determine the diameter of burnt shrubs, based on the extent of burnt branches. This method could not be applied at Wellington Plain because the fire had incinerated most shrubs, leaving few or no stems.
66	
67	# **Data analysis**
68	
69	Point quadrat data were explored using box and normal probability plots (Sokal & Rohlf 1995), which showed that all data met the assumptions for ANOVA. As the vegetation was sampled at the same sets of transects over time, we used repeated measures ANOVA (von Ende 1993). Mean intertussock gap size and mean tussock basal size, in burnt and unburnt grassland, were
70	
71	{3}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
72	
73	analysed by one-way ANOVA, whereas the biomass data were analysed by two-way (site fire) ANOVA. All analyses were undertaken using SYSTAT 8.0 (SPSS, Chicago).
74	
75	#### **RESULTS**
76	
77	## **Immediate fire impact**
78	
79	The Caledonia Fire affected most vegetation and all plant communities of both Holmes and Wellington Plains. The main impact was removal of vegetative cover and litter, resulting in high levels of bare ground and little vegetation cover. In burnt grassland at Holmes Plain, the average amount of CC1 was 17%, and the average amount of CC3 was 76%. This was a substantial decrease in the quality of cover at Holmes Plain compared with the prefire state (Fig. 2a). In burnt grassland at Wellington Plain, the respective figures were 11 and 85% (Fig. 2b). In burnt heathland at Wellington Plain, all shrubs were incinerated, resulting in virtually no vegetation (CC1 = 3%) and an almost complete cover of bare ground (CC3 = 96%; Fig. 2b).
80	
81	# **Post-fire regeneration**
82	
83	#### *Changes in vegetation cover and biomass*
84	
85	In burnt grassland, both at Holmes and Wellington Plains, and in burnt heathland at Wellington Plain, CC1 increased significantly, and CC3 decreased significantly over the 2.5-year study period, with most of the changes occurring in the first 18 months post-fire. There was a significant change in both CC1 and CC3 between February 1998 and May 1999, but between May 1999 and May 2000, there was little or no significant change in the average value of either cover class across sites (Fig. 2a). Similarly, there were significant changes in the cover classes in both grassland and heathland at Wellington Plain between January 1998 and May 1999, but relatively little change between May 1999 and May 2000 (Fig. 2b). By May 2000, the average CC3 in burnt grassland was 35% at Holmes Plain (Fig. 2a) and 25% at Wellington Plain (Fig. 2b). The respective figures for CC1 were 23 and 36%. In burnt heathland at Wellington Plain, average CC3 in May 2000 was 53%, and average CC1 was 16% (Fig. 2b).
86	
87	The post-fire increase in vegetation cover at both Holmes and Wellington Plains was primarily due to the rapid resprouting of snow grass tussocks and forbs (Figs 3a,4). The cover of *Poa* increased rapidly postfire in both grassland and heathland. At Holmes Plain it was 84% by January 1999 (Fig. 3a); at Wellington
88	
89	Plain it was approximately 65% in grassland by May 1999, and 55% in heathland (Fig. 4a,b). *Poa* cover remained at or near these levels at both sites until May 2000. This cover was almost completely due to surviving tussocks resprouting post-fire, rather than seedling establishment and growth. The rapid resprouting of the snow grasses was accompanied by pyrogenic flowering, which commenced in the year following the fire and occurred in virtually all tussocks. Forbs also re-established rapidly from perennating subterranean organs or seedlings. Forb cover was approximately 40% by January 1999 at both grassland sites, and by December 1999 at the heathland site (Figs 3a,4). Most forb cover was provided by *Asperula gunnii, Craspedia* spp. and *Leptorhynchos squamatus*. Some, such as *Bracteantha subundulata* and *Podolepis robusta*, occurred in distinct patches of 0.5–3 m<sup>2</sup> .
90	
91	In contrast to the rapid regeneration of snow grasses and forbs, shrubs in the heathland of Wellington Plain were slow to regenerate (Fig. 4b). Shrub cover increased at approximately 7% per annum, such that by May 2000, shrub cover was 17%. Although the prefire shrub cover at this site is unknown, it is likely to have been at least 50%, as the area had been mapped as closed heathland by Walsh *et al*. (1984). Shrubs, including the dominants, whether seedlings or resprouts, had not flowered after 2.5 years.
92	
93	The cover classes at the various prefire or unburnt grassland sites showed some intersite variation across the landscape and over time. In 1991 at Holmes Plain, at one site that was subsequently burnt in 1998, CC1 was 49% and CC3 was 21% (Fig. 2a). At the first site, total live vegetation cover was 80%, of which *Poa* provided three-quarters of the cover and forbs approximately one-quarter. The intertussock gaps at this site were generally occupied by forbs only, with little or no live grass foliage overlapping the gap, and only sparse litter within the gap. At the second site, unburnt by the Caledonia Fire, the respective CC1 and CC3 values in 1991 were 69 and 3%, and 73 and 5% in February
94	
95	**Fig. 1.** Location map of Holmes and Wellington Plains.
96	
97	{4}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
98	
99	1998. At this site, CC1 increased significantly between February 1998 and May 1999 (Fig. 2a). Total *Poa* cover at this site was 95–99%, and forb cover 40–45%; shrub cover was consistently < 5% (Fig. 3b). The intertussock gaps at this site were relatively small (< 10 cm diameter) and well-covered by live *Poa* foliage and forbs. At the unburnt Wellington grassland site in December 1999, CC1 was 74% and CC 3 was 4% (Fig. 2b).
100	
101	In May 2000, the biomass within burnt grassland was 8.6 t ha–1 at Holmes Plain, and 7.8 t ha-1 at Wellington Plain. Of this, an average of 5% was loose litter. The average biomass from burnt grassland at these two sites (8.2 t ha-1) was significantly lower (*P* < 0.001) than that
102	
103	of unburnt grassland (15.8 t ha–1). In unburnt grassland, 48% of the biomass was litter.
104	
105	# **Gaps and canopies**
106	
107	In grassland, the average basal diameter of snow grass tussocks was significantly lower (*P* < 0.001) in burnt grassland (32 and 24 mm at Holmes and Wellington Plains, respectively) than in unburnt grassland (87 mm at Holmes Plain; Table 1). Inter-tussock gap size and relative area was significantly higher, by a factor of 2–3, in burnt grassland than in unburnt grassland.
108

Cover class 3: (), burnt; (), unburnt. (b) (,-,), Cover class 1; (,,), cover class 3; (–––), burnt grassland; (....), burnt heathland; (–··–), unburnt grassland.
110

See the Terms and Conditions (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/terms-and-conditions) on Wiley Online Library for rules of use; OA articles are governed by the applicable Creative Commons License

113	{5}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
114	
115	**Fig. 3.** Cover of main growth forms on Holmes Plain in 1991 and 1998–2000. (a) Burnt grassland; (b) unburnt grassland. *y* axis = % Cover ( SEM; *n* = 10). (), *Poa*; (), forbs; (), shrubs.
116

124	
125	In open heathland at Holmes Plain, the estimated prefire cover of *Grevillea australis* was approximately 20%. These *Grevillea* shrubs were killed and the litter beneath their canopies, which is normally thick (up to 5 cm) and loose, was completely burnt. The death of these shrubs has effectively altered the structure of this community on Holmes Plain from heathland to grassland. At Wellington Plain, where most shrubs were incinerated, the dominant shrubs, although resprouters, were still in the early stages of regeneration and yet to develop a full canopy. As for *Grevillea* at Holmes Plain, the litter associated with the shrubs at Wellington Plain was completely burnt.
126	
127	# **DISCUSSION**
128	
129	#### **Fire regimes in alpine and subalpine environments in Australia**
130	
131	The available historical, meteorological and biological evidence points strongly to landscape-scale fire being a relatively rare event in Australian alpine and subalpine vegetation. McCarthy and Tolhurst (2000) estimated that the fire-weather conditions associated with the Caledonia Fire have occurred five times in the past century. Assuming a relative lack of ignition sources in treeless high mountain vegetation compared with
132	
133	**Fig. 4.** Cover of main growth forms on Wellington Plains 1998–2000. (a) burnt grassland (b) burnt heathland. *y* axis = % Cover ( SEM; *n* = 10). (), *Poa*; (), forbs; (), shrubs.
134	
135	{7}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
136	
137	forest vegetation, they concluded that a fire frequency of once or twice per century was 'a reasonable prediction'. In subalpine areas in the ACT and NSW, the data of Pryor (1939) and Raeder-Roitzsch and Phillips (1958) are consistent with this conclusion.
138	
139	This relatively low frequency of fire in Australian alpine landscapes is a function of the generally low to moderate fire weather conditions that occur at high altitude compared with landscapes at lower altitudes (Gill & Moore 1990). Fire in alpine and subalpine vegetation occurs only in exceptional circumstances, such as when drought is coupled with extreme fire-weather conditions. The fire discussed here has therefore provided a rare opportunity for detailed monitoring, in both the immediate post-fire period and the longer term, of the ecological processes governing post-fire vegetation change in high mountain treeless vegetation.

1954; Carr & Turner 1959a; Lawrence 1999). These practices all increased the frequency of fire in alpine and subalpine vegetation (Pryor 1939; Stretton 1946; Raeder-Roitzsch & Phillips 1958; Leigh *et al*. 1987; Banks 1989; Kershaw & Strickland 1989; Lawrence 1999). On mainland Australia, prescribed fire in treeless subalpine and alpine vegetation was banned in the 1940s and 1950s, as its use was linked clearly to land degradation in the high mountain catchments (Australian Academy of Science 1957; Costin *et al*. 1959; Williams & Costin 1994).

In Victoria, there are few detailed data on the occurrence of fires and their effects on alpine and subalpine plant communities. Extensive fires in treeless vegetation are known to have occurred on two occasions in the 20th century. According to Carr & Turner (1959a) '. . . small fires spread onto the high plains from the neighbouring slopes prior to 1939, such as in 1926, but these fires were of minor importance'. In contrast, the State-wide fires of 1939 burnt approximately 80% of the snow gum country on the Bogong High Plains above approximately 1500 m a.s.l. (Carr & Turner 1959a). Although these fires burnt much treeless subalpine and alpine vegetation, that is, heathland, grassland, and wetland (Carr & Turner 1959a), we do not know the precise extent or severity of these fires. In 1985, a fire at Mount Buffalo burnt approximately 11 000 ha of lowland and forested foothill vegetation, and approximately 150 ha of treeless subalpine heathland, grassland and wetland (Wahren *et al*. 1999). The subject of the present paper is an extensive fire that occurred in the south-eastern parts of the Victorian Alpine National Park in January 1998: the 'Caledonia Fire'.

Subsequent to the last glaciation, Australian alpine environments have evolved in response to relatively small-scale disturbances (1 m<sup>2</sup> –1 ha) such as localized frost heave, wind blasting and insect herbivory. Larger scale disturbances such as fire and extensive grazing by large vertebrate herbivores over square kilometres of country are rare or non-existent (Williams 1990; Williams & Costin 1994). Under such a native regime of small-scale disturbances, Australian alpine environments are characterized by a high cover of vegetation (normally close to 100%) and relatively little exposed bare soil (< 1–2%; Australian Academy of Science 1957; Costin 1958; Williams & Costin 1994). The removal of vegetation and litter by fire, and the consequent exposure of bare soil, has major implications in Australian alpine landscapes, because exposure of alpine soils is undesirable for soil conservation purposes, and subsequent regeneration to adequate soil cover is slow (Wahren *et al*. 1994; Williams & Costin 1994).

In the present paper, we summarize the early postfire changes in vegetation and ground cover conditions that have occurred in grassland and heathland on Holmes and Wellington Plains, two of the larger high plains burnt in the Caledonia Fire (Fig. 1). We focus on the first 2 years post-fire because there have been no detailed, quantitative studies of early post-fire responses in Australian alpine landscapes following fires of such magnitude. The specific aim is to document the changes in vegetation cover, the amount of bare ground, and changes to gaps that have occurred in grassland and heathland over the first 2 years post-fire. Both communities are extensive in treeless high mountain environments in Australia. Within each, the amount of bare ground and both the quality and quantity of vegetation cover, and the nature of gaps created by the death of grass tussocks or shrubs, are critical determinants of both vegetation change and landscape condition in Australian high mountain landscapes (Wahren *et al*. 1994; Williams & Costin 1994).

#### **Fire and study sites**

The Caledonia Fire started on 31 December 1997, from an abandoned campfire on the Caledonia River, in mixed lowland eucalypt forest. 1 January 1998 was a day of extreme fire weather: the predicted forest fire danger index (Luke & McArthur 1978) for the nearby town of Heyfield was 50 (Tolhurst 1998). Fire weather and drought conditions at this time were broadly similar to those of other years in the past century when widespread fires occurred in Victoria: 1983, 1967, 1964, 1939 and 1926 (McCarthy & Tolhurst 2000). The fire burnt approximately 35 000 ha of the Carey Forest, of which approximately 22 000 ha was within the Alpine National Park, and approximately 3000 ha was treeless subalpine vegetation.

The landscape above approximately 1400 m is a mosaic of high ridges, wooded slopes, rolling grassy plains and wetlands. The treeless plains and surrounding snow gum (*Eucalyptus pauciflora*) woodlands have been grazed during summer and autumn by free ranging cattle since the late 19th century and cattle were present at the time of the fire. Sporadic grazing continued for 3 months post-fire, but grazing was excluded from the fire-affected area for the 1998–1999 and 1999–2000 seasons.

The fires were intense crown fires in both the eucalypt forests of the foothills and the subalpine snow gum woodlands. In the treeless vegetation, fire intensity was unknown, but field observations indicated that the fire at Wellington Plain was more intense and burnt more of the vegetation than at Holmes Plain. At Holmes and Wellington Plains, > 90% of the grassland, heathland and snow gum woodlands were burnt, and the subalpine bogs were also extensively burnt. This represents the most extensive fire in alpine and subalpine vegetation since 1939 (McCarthy & Tolhurst 2000).

{2}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

# **METHODS**

#### **Monitoring sites**

At the end of January 1998, 3 weeks after the fire, monitoring sites were established at Holmes Plain (146°45-14--E, 37°24-32--S; 1400 m a.s.l.) and Wellington Plain (146°49-54--E, 37°29-46--S; 1480 m a.s.l.). These plains were selected because they were representative of the extensive subalpine high plains in this region of the Victorian Alps (Walsh *et al*. 1984, 1986) and, in the case of Holmes Plain, because two sites had been established in grassland in 1991 as part of a general monitoring program in the high country. At both sites, the soil was alpine humus soil, a wellstructured organic loam that is acid, nutrient poor, and is typical of most alpine and subalpine grasslands and heathlands in mainland Australia (Williams & Costin 1994). One of these sites was burnt, the other was outside the fire perimeter; both sites were used for the present study. Extra sites were established in burnt heathland and grassland at both Holmes and Wellington Plains, and in an unburnt area of grassland at Wellington Plain, close to the burnt grassland. This unburnt grassland was within the fire perimeter. Using this network of sites, the changes in the burnt grassland over time could be compared with those in longunburnt grassland. Unfortunately, there were no suitable unburnt heathland sites.

# **Estimation of ground cover and biomass**

Point quadrats, sampled along permanent transects (Kent & Coker 1992), were used to record species composition and ground cover conditions. Transects were 10 m long with points 4 mm in diameter, and 20 cm apart (50 points per transect). This method has been widely used for many decades to estimate the cover of individual species and life forms (grasses, forbs and shrubs) in treeless vegetation in Australia (Carr & Turner 1959b; Wimbush & Costin 1979a,b,c; Wahren *et al*. 1994). Ground cover at each point was rated in terms of three cover classes (Wahren *et al*. 1994). Cover class 1 (CC1) is fixed litter or dense live vegetation, cover class (CC2) provides intermediate vegetation cover but the litter is loose, and cover class (CC3) consists of bare ground or sparse vegetation and/or thin (< 5 mm thick) loose litter. Live vegetation and litter were measured together in all cover classes, as both are important for soil protection in Australian alpine environments (Wahren *et al*. 1994).

In the Holmes Plain grassland, there were 40 transects (including 13 from 1991) distributed over an area of approximately 40 ha of burnt grassland. There were an additional 10 transects (six from 1991) in the unburnt grassland, over an area of approximately 2 ha; burnt and unburnt grassland sites were approximately 1 km apart. At Wellington Plain, there were 40 transects established in burnt heathland over an area of approximately 40 ha, and 10 transects in burnt grassland over an area of 2 ha. Subsequent to January 1998, the vegetation was remeasured along the transects in May 1998, January, May and December 1999, and late April/early May 2000. In December 1999, four transects were set up in a patch of unburnt grassland at Wellington Plain, 200 m from the burnt grassland; these were remeasured in May 2000.

Above-ground biomass was sampled in March–May 2000, using direct harvest from 10 0.25-m<sup>2</sup> quadrats distributed at random in both burnt and unburnt grassland of Holmes and Wellington Plains. Samples were separated in the field into standing vegetation and litter components. Biomass samples were not collected from heathland because of the likely damage to regenerating areas where there was at least 50% bare ground and small shrub seedlings.

#### **Assessment of grass tussock basal area, intertussock gaps and prefire shrub cover**

In addition to changes in bare ground and vegetation cover, we documented changes in the size and type of gap, both interdominant and within-canopy, in grassland and heathland. Such gaps are important determinants of ecological processes in these communities (Williams & Ashton 1988; Williams 1992). The area occupied by intertussock gaps and *Poa* tussock bases was estimated by line intercepts (Bonham 1989). Intercepted basal tussock length was measured by using a metal pin, 4 mm in diameter, placed vertically against the edge of the tussock. Ten randomly distributed 10-m long transects were sampled in both burnt and unburnt grassland at Holmes Plain, and in burnt grassland at Wellington Plain. As there were no prefire data of shrub cover in open heathland, this was estimated at Holmes Plain by using line intercepts to determine the diameter of burnt shrubs, based on the extent of burnt branches. This method could not be applied at Wellington Plain because the fire had incinerated most shrubs, leaving few or no stems.

# **Data analysis**

Point quadrat data were explored using box and normal probability plots (Sokal & Rohlf 1995), which showed that all data met the assumptions for ANOVA. As the vegetation was sampled at the same sets of transects over time, we used repeated measures ANOVA (von Ende 1993). Mean intertussock gap size and mean tussock basal size, in burnt and unburnt grassland, were

{3}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

analysed by one-way ANOVA, whereas the biomass data were analysed by two-way (site fire) ANOVA. All analyses were undertaken using SYSTAT 8.0 (SPSS, Chicago).

#### **RESULTS**

## **Immediate fire impact**

The Caledonia Fire affected most vegetation and all plant communities of both Holmes and Wellington Plains. The main impact was removal of vegetative cover and litter, resulting in high levels of bare ground and little vegetation cover. In burnt grassland at Holmes Plain, the average amount of CC1 was 17%, and the average amount of CC3 was 76%. This was a substantial decrease in the quality of cover at Holmes Plain compared with the prefire state (Fig. 2a). In burnt grassland at Wellington Plain, the respective figures were 11 and 85% (Fig. 2b). In burnt heathland at Wellington Plain, all shrubs were incinerated, resulting in virtually no vegetation (CC1 = 3%) and an almost complete cover of bare ground (CC3 = 96%; Fig. 2b).

# **Post-fire regeneration**

#### *Changes in vegetation cover and biomass*

In burnt grassland, both at Holmes and Wellington Plains, and in burnt heathland at Wellington Plain, CC1 increased significantly, and CC3 decreased significantly over the 2.5-year study period, with most of the changes occurring in the first 18 months post-fire. There was a significant change in both CC1 and CC3 between February 1998 and May 1999, but between May 1999 and May 2000, there was little or no significant change in the average value of either cover class across sites (Fig. 2a). Similarly, there were significant changes in the cover classes in both grassland and heathland at Wellington Plain between January 1998 and May 1999, but relatively little change between May 1999 and May 2000 (Fig. 2b). By May 2000, the average CC3 in burnt grassland was 35% at Holmes Plain (Fig. 2a) and 25% at Wellington Plain (Fig. 2b). The respective figures for CC1 were 23 and 36%. In burnt heathland at Wellington Plain, average CC3 in May 2000 was 53%, and average CC1 was 16% (Fig. 2b).

The post-fire increase in vegetation cover at both Holmes and Wellington Plains was primarily due to the rapid resprouting of snow grass tussocks and forbs (Figs 3a,4). The cover of *Poa* increased rapidly postfire in both grassland and heathland. At Holmes Plain it was 84% by January 1999 (Fig. 3a); at Wellington

Plain it was approximately 65% in grassland by May 1999, and 55% in heathland (Fig. 4a,b). *Poa* cover remained at or near these levels at both sites until May 2000. This cover was almost completely due to surviving tussocks resprouting post-fire, rather than seedling establishment and growth. The rapid resprouting of the snow grasses was accompanied by pyrogenic flowering, which commenced in the year following the fire and occurred in virtually all tussocks. Forbs also re-established rapidly from perennating subterranean organs or seedlings. Forb cover was approximately 40% by January 1999 at both grassland sites, and by December 1999 at the heathland site (Figs 3a,4). Most forb cover was provided by *Asperula gunnii, Craspedia* spp. and *Leptorhynchos squamatus*. Some, such as *Bracteantha subundulata* and *Podolepis robusta*, occurred in distinct patches of 0.5–3 m<sup>2</sup> .

In contrast to the rapid regeneration of snow grasses and forbs, shrubs in the heathland of Wellington Plain were slow to regenerate (Fig. 4b). Shrub cover increased at approximately 7% per annum, such that by May 2000, shrub cover was 17%. Although the prefire shrub cover at this site is unknown, it is likely to have been at least 50%, as the area had been mapped as closed heathland by Walsh *et al*. (1984). Shrubs, including the dominants, whether seedlings or resprouts, had not flowered after 2.5 years.

The cover classes at the various prefire or unburnt grassland sites showed some intersite variation across the landscape and over time. In 1991 at Holmes Plain, at one site that was subsequently burnt in 1998, CC1 was 49% and CC3 was 21% (Fig. 2a). At the first site, total live vegetation cover was 80%, of which *Poa* provided three-quarters of the cover and forbs approximately one-quarter. The intertussock gaps at this site were generally occupied by forbs only, with little or no live grass foliage overlapping the gap, and only sparse litter within the gap. At the second site, unburnt by the Caledonia Fire, the respective CC1 and CC3 values in 1991 were 69 and 3%, and 73 and 5% in February
